comparator.academicYear: Indicative prospective-student sequence: year 1 labelled 2027–2028, year 2 labelled 2028–2029 and year 3 labelled 2029–2030; checked 2026-10-08
comparator.sourceNotes: The official prospectus shows 60 EC in each year. Year 1 comprises twelve compulsory 5-EC courses; the 0-EC mentoring and academic-writing activities and the optional 5-EC language intensification for entrants without a school examination in Greek or Latin are excluded. Year 2 combines six required 5-EC courses with two restricted-choice Humanities minors (15 EC each). The domestic year-three route has four required 5-EC courses, a 10-EC Classics bachelor thesis and 30 EC of genuinely free elective space. Its 5-EC personal-development completion remains a separate required credit-bearing component. The three current indicative page labels now describe a prospective 2027-entry sequence (2027–2028, 2028–2029, 2029–2030). This is the published prospective domestic pathway, not an adopted guaranteed timetable for a Fall 2026 entrant. The programme overview and all three indicative year pages were rechecked on 13 October 2026; the component list, weights and domestic route remain current.

selection.assessment: Two complete related-fields programmes are defensible. The first combines classical literature and myth in translation, rhetoric, ancient philosophy, Greek archaeology, history, material culture and reception. The second follows the independently evidenced question of how antiquity shaped later politics, law and citizenship; twelve courses / 90 EC differ in each direction. A third route centred on Greek and Latin language, philology and original texts fails because UCR has no ancient-language or classical-linguistics sequence. The separate teaching direction also fails for lack of Greek/Latin subject preparation and didactics; this is an academic-content judgment, not a rejection based only on professional qualification.

alternatives.label: Classical antiquity through literature, rhetoric, philosophy & archaeology
alternatives.concept: The closest feasible UCR response to Radboud Classics combines classical literature and myth in translation, rhetoric and stylistics, ancient philosophy, Greek archaeology, imperial history, material culture and the reception of antiquity. It is a related-fields programme and cannot reproduce the comparator's cumulative Greek and Latin language, linguistics, translation and original-text sequence.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum is organised around classical literature and myth, rhetoric, ancient philosophy, Greek archaeology, imperial history and the later reception of antiquity. The label states those related fields and does not imply Greek or Latin proficiency.
progression: Introductory literary studies, classical rhetoric, Western philosophy and world archaeology are placed in the first year, before the 200-level work on Greek archaeology, stylistics, myth and epic, empires and ancient warfare, and before the third-year courses on ancient democratic heritage, persuasive communication, adaptation, interpretive theory, art-historical research and the archival research seminar. No scheduled course carries a formal prerequisite, every course is offered in its assigned term, and the one 100-level course placed in year two, Introduction to Western Art History, is a deliberate entry point into the Renaissance reception strand rather than a displaced foundation.

alternatives.label: Antiquity, democracy & the politics of the present
alternatives.concept: A genuinely different question-led route centred on how ancient arrangements of democracy, citizenship, empire and political membership shaped later societies. It connects the material and intellectual history of antiquity to comparative politics, law, conflict and historical research rather than organising the curriculum around literary interpretation.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum uses archaeology, empire and ancient political philosophy as its starting point, then concentrates on law, comparative politics, international relations and modern historical research. The label reflects that question-led structure rather than presenting it as a Classics degree.
progression: Law, Society & Justice, political philosophy and Western philosophy open the first year and Law, Society & Justice precedes every law course that formally requires it. World archaeology, Greek archaeology, public international law and ethics follow in semester two; comparative politics, modern history, empires and human rights in semester three; and the 300-level work on private law, EU politics, ancient democratic heritage, peace and conflict, EU law, historical research and art-historical research in years three. Every formal prerequisite is completed earlier and every course is offered in its assigned term.
alternatives.distinctness: The alternatives differ by twelve courses / 90 EC in each direction. The closest response concentrates on literature, rhetoric, stylistics, creative reception and art history, while the second replaces that block with a coherent sequence in law, comparative politics, international relations, conflict and modern historical inquiry. The substitutions follow from the evidenced democracy-and-political-reception question.

notes.text: Radboud Classics combines cumulative Greek and Latin language acquisition, translation, linguistics and advanced reading of original texts with literature, history, philosophy and archaeology. UCR can approach classical antiquity through literature in translation, rhetoric, philosophy, archaeology, heritage, history, law and politics, but it does not teach Greek or Latin. The UCR programmes therefore offer related perspectives rather than a full Classics curriculum.

The external programme follows a fixed Greek-and-Latin disciplinary sequence, alongside two restricted Humanities minors, 30 EC of free choice and a 10-EC thesis. UCR assembles related material across individually selected courses and has no scheduled thesis; optional independent research is shown only as the standardized comparison element.
